segments.title: Why refrigerated cargo ships mattered in 1939
segments.summary: SS Tairoa shows why refrigerated merchant ships carrying meat and other perishables mattered during the Second World War.
segments.body: SS Tairoa was a refrigerated cargo ship of roughly 8,000 gross tons. Ships like her carried meat and other perishables across oceans, an important part of wartime supply during the Battle of the Atlantic. Britain and its partners depended on this traffic, so German commerce raiders had strong reason to target refrigerated ships. Tairoa's sinking removed both a merchant hull and cargo capacity from that long-distance supply network.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies Tairoa as a refrigerated cargo ship and links such ships to the movement of meat, perishables, and other supplies across the oceans.

segments.title: Tairoa's Brisbane-to-London cargo route
segments.summary: Tairoa's regular Brisbane-to-London service shows how a refrigerated ship could carry its principal cargo alongside whatever general cargo fit in the remaining space.
segments.body: Tairoa was making her usual Brisbane-to-London voyage. Her refrigerated holds carried the principal cargo, while "general cargo" meant other goods packed into whatever space remained. The ship therefore combined specialist refrigerated work with a mixed load of additional goods. Her ordinary route was part of the long-distance merchant traffic exposed to German surface raiders in the South Atlantic.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Tairoa's regular Brisbane-to-London route and explains the flexible meaning of general cargo aboard a refrigerated ship.

segments.title: Cummings keeps Tairoa's warning on the air
segments.summary: Radio officer Cummings repeatedly rebuilds and resumes Tairoa's raider warning while Admiral Graf Spee uses anti-aircraft and main guns to silence it.
segments.body: Radio officer Cummings began transmitting a raider warning as Admiral Graf Spee attacked. After 37 mm anti-aircraft fire disabled his first position, he found another space, assembled a makeshift radio, and resumed transmitting. German 5.9-inch gunfire finally stopped the signal. The Germans then removed Tairoa's crew, and Graf Spee used more shells and a torpedo to sink the merchant ship. Cummings's persistence turned the encounter into a fresh position report for the British hunting forces.

evidence.note: The transcript recounts Cummings's repeated transmissions, the German attempts to silence him, and the gunfire and torpedo used against Tairoa.

segments.title: What Graf Spee gained from Tairoa's routing papers
segments.summary: Routing papers left aboard Tairoa could reveal merchant routes and choke points, although those same places were likely to be guarded by the Royal Navy.
segments.body: Some papers were left aboard Tairoa in the rush to send distress signals, and German personnel recovered them. The documents could reveal shipping routes and help identify points where merchant traffic gathered. Their value had a limit: the Royal Navy could read the same geography and guard the likely choke points. Graf Spee could use the captured information, but operating near the locations it revealed carried its own risk.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses the captured papers, the routes and concentration points they might reveal, and the likelihood that such choke points would be guarded.

segments.title: Tairoa's signal tightens the hunt for Graf Spee
segments.summary: Tairoa's warning gives British hunting forces a fresh position for Graf Spee, sending ships north and pushing Captain Hans Langsdorff west across the Atlantic.
segments.body: Tairoa's distress signal gave the Royal Navy another accurate position for Admiral Graf Spee. British ships operating farther south drove north at the greatest practical speed. That movement made the African coast increasingly dangerous for Captain Hans Langsdorff, who had to leave the area. Graf Spee then headed west across the Atlantic, one step in the operational sequence that preceded the Battle of the River Plate.

evidence.note: The transcript says the signal fixed Graf Spee's position, describes British ships racing north, and explains Langsdorff's need to leave the African coast.
